title: Contrast-tip scarf
subtitle: A plain scarf with a bold contrast colour at each end.
excerpt: A scarf knitted flat in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide by 160 cm long. The main body is worked in the primary colour with a 15 cm contrast-colour section at each end. The colour change is a single clean join; no stranding or intarsia is needed.
sourceNotes: Tipped scarves with contrasting ends appear in Victorian knitting catalogues including Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. The contrast-tip construction is also documented in early 20th-century pattern leaflets.
heroPrompt: A finished contrast-tip scarf in a main colour of camel aran-weight yarn with bold navy contrast tips at each end, photographed hanging straight showing the two clear colour blocks at each tip.

glossaryTerms.definition: The point where one yarn is ended and a new colour is begun. In a contrast-tip scarf the colour join happens twice: once near the cast-on end and once near the bind-off end.
A method of joining two yarn ends by looping each through the other and threading back through the plies before cutting, creating a secure join with no tail to weave in.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a scarf knitted flat in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide and 160 cm long when blocked. The first 15 cm is worked in the contrast colour (CC), then a single clean
colour join

switches to the main colour (MC) for the 130 cm body, then a second colour join returns to CC for the final 15 cm tip. The contrast-tip construction requires no stranding, no intarsia, and no mosaic slipping: just two colour joins in a plain stocking stitch fabric.

Stocking stitch was chosen for the cleanest display of the contrast tips. A stocking stitch scarf curls at the edges unless blocked; the pattern includes a simple garter stitch selvedge on each edge (knit the first and last stitch of every row in both colours) to reduce curl without a full border. The finished scarf needs about 290 m (approximately 170 g) of MC and 80 m (approximately 50 g) of CC.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight yarn, contrast colour (CC)
items.substitutions: A strongly contrasting colour gives the boldest tip effect.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 1.1 cm at this stitch count. Row gauge is important for the 15 cm tip sections: 36 rows produce 15 cm at 24 rows per 10 cm.
Pattern
Cast on and first tip
Use the
long-tail cast-on

in CC to place 36 stitches on the needle. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 36 stitches: (15.7 x 36) / 10 + 15 = 56.5 + 15 = about 72 cm. Leave at least 72 cm of CC tail.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 36 stitches on the needle.
First tip (36 rows in CC, approx. 15 cm):
RS rows: K1 (selvedge), K34, K1 (selvedge). WS rows: K1 (selvedge), P34, K1 (selvedge). Work 36 rows total.
Colour join to MC
At the start of a RS row, join MC using a
Russian join

or simply by holding the CC tail and MC tail together for the first 4 stitches, then dropping CC. Leave a 10 cm CC tail to weave in. Work the remainder of the RS row in MC. Continue in MC for 312 rows (approx. 130 cm), maintaining the K1 selvedge on each edge every row.
Stitch count check-in: at the halfway mark (approximately row 192 of the full body) you should have 36 stitches on the needle.
Colour join back to CC and second tip
After 312 rows of MC, join CC in the same way. Work 36 rows in CC to complete the second tip. Bind off in CC.
Common faults

Loose stitch at the colour join. The first stitch after a colour join is typically loose because the new yarn is not yet under tension. Hold both the new yarn and the tail snugly against the needle for the first two stitches after the join, then release the tail and continue normally.

Stocking stitch curling at the long edges. The K1 garter selvedge on each edge reduces but does not completely eliminate curl. Block the finished scarf flat and pin the long edges straight. The blocking holds permanently on wool; synthetic yarns re-curl.
Tip sections of unequal length. Count the rows in each tip section: 36 RS rows + 36 WS rows = 36 total row pairs. Use a row counter if needed.
Finishing
Weave in all tails at the two colour joins and the cast-on and bind-off. Block flat to 20 x 160 cm, pinning the long edges straight.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry. Reblock if the edges curl after washing.
What to try next

The gradient scarf replaces the two clean joins with a series of short alternating stripes that blend gradually across the full length. The intarsia stripe scarf adds vertical colour blocks across the width rather than horizontal blocks along the length.
